dataset_metadata.disclaimer: New AI-generated English drafts of the recorded Classical Chinese; not scholarly reviewed. Original source interpretations are not verified geometry or modern etymology.

shuowen:1.text: At the primordial beginning, the Way was established in One; it created and divided heaven and earth, transforming and completing the myriad things. All characters in the 一 category are formed from 一.

shuowen:2.text: Beginning. Formed from 一 and 兀.

shuowen:3.text: The summit; supremely high, with nothing above it. Formed from 一 and 大.

shuowen:4.text: Great. Formed from 一, with 不 indicating the sound.

shuowen:5.text: One who governs people. Formed from 一 and 史; 史 also indicates the sound.

shuowen:6.text: High. This is the ancient form of 上, an indicative graph. All characters in the 丄 category are formed from 丄.

shuowen:7.text: Discerning; the title of the ruler of all under heaven. Formed from 丄, with 朿 indicating the sound.

shuowen:8.text: Extensive. Formed from 二; the explanation is missing. 方 indicates the sound.

shuowen:10.text: Heaven displays signs revealing good and ill fortune, thereby instructing people. Formed from 二 (the ancient form of 上). The three hanging strokes are the sun, moon and stars. Observing heavenly patterns reveals seasonal changes. 示 concerns divine affairs. All characters in the 示 category are formed from 示.

shuowen:11.text: The reigning sovereign's taboo personal name.

shuowen:12.text: To tread or carry out; that by which one serves the spirits and brings blessings. Formed from 示 and 豊; 豊 also indicates the sound.

shuowen:13.text: Auspicious ritual. Formed from 示, with 喜 indicating the sound.

shuowen:14.text: To receive blessings through sincerity. Formed from 示, with 眞 indicating the sound.

shuowen:15.text: Blessing. Formed from 示, with 彔 indicating the sound.

shuowen:16.text: Blessing. Formed from 示, with 虒 indicating the sound.

shuowen:17.text: An auspicious sign. Formed from 示, with 貞 indicating the sound.

shuowen:18.text: Blessing. Formed from 示, with 羊 indicating the sound. Another explanation says: good.

shuowen:19.text: Blessing. Formed from 示, with 止 indicating the sound.

shuowen:20.text: Divine aid. Formed from 示, with 畐 indicating the sound.

shuowen:21.text: Assistance. Formed from 示, with 右 indicating the sound.

shuowen:22.text: Auspicious. Formed from 示, with 其 indicating the sound.

shuowen:23.text: Respect. Formed from 示, with 氐 indicating the sound.

shuowen:24.text: Peace and blessing. Formed from 示, with 是 indicating the sound. The Changes says: “Peace and blessing have already been established.”

shuowen:25.text: Heavenly spirits, which draw forth the myriad things. Formed from 示 and 申.

shuowen:26.text: Earth spirits, which raise forth the myriad things. Formed from 示, with 氏 indicating the sound.

shuowen:27.text: Divine or mysterious. Formed from 示, with 必 indicating the sound.

shuowen:28.text: Abstinence and purification. Formed from 示, with an abbreviated 齊 indicating the sound.

shuowen:29.text: A pure sacrifice. Another explanation calls offering with concentrated intent 禋. Formed from 示, with 垔 indicating the sound.

shuowen:30.text: To offer sacrifice. Formed from 示 and a hand holding meat.

shuowen:31.text: To sacrifice without ceasing. Formed from 示, with 巳 indicating the sound.

shuowen:32.text: To burn firewood in a blaze as a sacrifice to heavenly spirits. Formed from 示, with 此 indicating the sound. The Book of Yu says: “Arriving at Daizong, he offered the firewood sacrifice.”

shuowen:33.text: To sacrifice to heavenly spirits according to the category of the occasion. Formed from 示, with 類 indicating the sound.

shuowen:34.text: An ancestor represented in a discontinued or dismantled ancestral temple (contrasted with 祔, associated with a new ancestral temple). Formed from 示, with 危 indicating the sound.

shuowen:35.text: For one who has died later to share sacrificial offerings with earlier ancestors. Formed from 示, with 付 indicating the sound.

shuowen:36.text: The founding ancestral temple. Formed from 示, with 且 indicating the sound.

shuowen:37.text: A sacrifice inside the gate, where the ancestors linger. Formed from 示, with 彭 indicating the sound. The Odes says: “The invocator sacrifices at the 𥛱.”

shuowen:38.text: A sacrifice announcing a matter. Formed from 示, with 告 indicating the sound.

shuowen:39.text: An ancestral-temple spirit tablet. The Rites of Zhou has suburban, ancestral and stone chambers. Another explanation says that grandees use stone for their tablets. Formed from 示 and 石; 石 also indicates the sound.

shuowen:40.text: To sacrifice a piglet to the Director of Destinies. Formed from 示, with 比 indicating the sound. Han law says: “Offer the piglet sacrifice to the Director of Destinies.”

shuowen:41.text: The spring sacrifice is called 祠: its offerings are few, but its ritual words many. Formed from 示, with 司 indicating the sound. In mid-spring this sacrifice uses no animal victims, but jade tablets and discs, hides and silk.

shuowen:42.text: The summer sacrifice. Formed from 示, with 勺 indicating the sound.

shuowen:43.text: A discerning sacrifice. Formed from 示, with 帝 indicating the sound. The Rites of Zhou says: “One 禘 every five years.”

shuowen:44.text: A great joint sacrifice to ancestors, close and distant in kinship and time. Formed from 示 and 合. The Rites of Zhou says: “One 祫 every three years.”

shuowen:45.text: A libation sacrifice. Formed from 示, with 果 indicating the sound.

shuowen:46.text: Repeated sacrifices. Formed from 示, with 毳 indicating the sound. Read like 䄟 in “pounding wheat into 䄟.”

shuowen:47.text: The officiant who assists with the words at a sacrifice. Formed from 示 and a person's mouth. Another explanation derives it from abbreviated 兌. The Changes says: “兌 represents the mouth and the shaman.”

shuowen:48.text: A ritual invocation used in healing, corresponding to 祝由. Formed from 示, with 畱 indicating the sound.

shuowen:49.text: A sacrifice to remove evil. Formed from 示, with 犮 indicating the sound.

shuowen:50.text: To seek blessings. Formed from 示, with 斤 indicating the sound.

shuowen:51.text: To report a matter and seek blessings. Formed from 示, with 壽 indicating the sound.

shuowen:52.text: To mark out an enclosure with cord and bundled reeds, imploring sun, moon, stars, mountains and rivers to avert wind, rain, snow, frost, flood, drought and epidemic. Formed from 示, with abbreviated 榮 indicating the sound. Another explanation: 禜 means to guard, preventing disasters. The Record of Rites says: “雩 and 禜: sacrifices concerning flood and drought.”

shuowen:53.text: An apotropaic sacrifice involving dismembered victims to ward off pestilence and calamity. The text attributes its invention to Suiren, in connection with a rite to avert disaster from his son; Duan Yucai remarks that the story is otherwise unattested. Formed from 示, with 襄 indicating the sound.

shuowen:54.text: A sacrifice gathering blessings. Formed from 示 and 會; 會 also indicates the sound. The Rites of Zhou says: “The invocations used in the 禬 sacrifice.”

shuowen:55.text: To sacrifice to Heaven. Formed from 示, with 單 indicating the sound.

shuowen:56.text: To sacrifice. Formed from 示, with 御 indicating the sound.

shuowen:57.text: To sacrifice. Formed from 示, with 𠯑 indicating the sound.

shuowen:58.text: A sacrifice. Formed from 示, with 某 indicating the sound.

shuowen:59.text: Sacrificial equipment. Formed from 示, with 胥 indicating the sound.

shuowen:60.text: Meat from the earth-altar sacrifice, placed in a clam shell, hence called 祳. The Son of Heaven personally sends it to people of his own surname. Formed from 示, with 辰 indicating the sound. The Spring and Autumn commentary says: “Shi Shang came to deliver 祳.”

shuowen:61.text: To perform the 祴 music in the ancestral temple. Formed from 示, with 戒 indicating the sound.

shuowen:62.text: When an army halts on campaign, fearing disrespect toward the local spirit, its members dismount and sacrifice; this is called 禡. Formed from 示, with 馬 indicating the sound. The Rites of Zhou says: “Perform 禡 in the land being attacked.”

shuowen:63.text: A prayer sacrifice concerning livestock and horses. Formed from 示, with 周 indicating the sound. The Odes says: “Having performed 禡 and 禂.”

shuowen:64.text: The lord of the soil. Formed from 示 and 土. The Spring and Autumn commentary says: “Gonggong's son Goulong became the earth-altar spirit.” The Rites of Zhou says: “Twenty-five households form an earth-altar community; each plants a tree suited to its soil.”

shuowen:65.text: A sacrifice on the road. Formed from 示, with 昜 indicating the sound.

shuowen:66.text: Omen-bearing vapors, especially inauspicious atmospheric manifestations. Formed from 示, with an abbreviated 㑴 indicating the sound. The Spring and Autumn commentary speaks of seeing red and black portentous vapors.

shuowen:67.text: Harm: the spirits do not bestow blessing. Formed from 示, with 咼 indicating the sound.

shuowen:68.text: A calamity caused by spirits. Formed from 示 and 出.

shuowen:69.text: When the earth produces things contrary to their normal nature, this is 䄏. Formed from 示, with 芺 indicating the sound.

shuowen:70.text: To examine clearly and calculate. Formed from two 示. The Lost Book of Zhou says: “The officers apportion the people's 祘”; that is, divide equally by calculation. Read like 筭.

shuowen:71.text: Taboos concerning good and ill fortune. Formed from 示, with 林 indicating the sound.

shuowen:72.text: A sacrifice on removing mourning dress. Formed from 示, with 覃 indicating the sound.

shuowen:73.text: The temple of one's immediate ancestor. Formed from 示, with 爾 indicating the sound. One edition says it is the ancient form 𥜬.

shuowen:74.text: A temple to which ancestral tablets are transferred. Formed from 示, with 兆 indicating the sound.

shuowen:75.text: A deity of the Hu peoples. Formed from 示, with 天 indicating the sound.

shuowen:76.text: Blessing. Formed from 示, with 乍 indicating the sound.

shuowen:77.text: The way of heaven, earth and humanity. Formed from the number three. All characters in the 三 category are formed from 三.

shuowen:78.text: That to which all under heaven turn. Dong Zhongshu said: “The ancient makers of writing called three strokes joined through their middle 王. The three are heaven, earth and humanity; the king connects all three.” Confucius said: “One stroke running through three makes 王.” All characters in the 王 category are formed from 王. [Li Yangbing said: “The middle stroke is close to the upper one: the king models himself on Heaven.”]

shuowen:79.text: The month of the surplus fraction; there are two intercalations in five years. During the rite announcing the new moon, the Son of Heaven occupies the ancestral temple; in an intercalary month he occupies the gateway. Formed from 王 inside 門. The Rites of Zhou says: “In an intercalary month the king occupies the gateway throughout the month.”

shuowen:80.text: Great. Formed from 自. 自 means beginning. The earliest sovereigns were the Three Sovereigns, great rulers. 自 is pronounced like 鼻; common speech now calls the firstborn child 鼻子.

shuowen:81.text: Beautiful stone. It has five virtues: warm moist luster embodies benevolence; its internal texture can be known from outside, embodying righteousness; its expansive, spreading sound is heard afar, embodying wisdom; breaking rather than bending embodies courage; sharp edges that do not injure embody purity. It depicts three linked pieces of jade; 丨 is their string. All characters in the 玉 category are formed from 玉. [Yangbing said: “The three strokes are evenly spaced, like strung jade.”]

shuowen:82.text: Jade. Formed from 玉, with 尞 indicating the sound.

shuowen:83.text: Jade. Formed from 玉, with 雚 indicating the sound. The Spring and Autumn commentary says: “A 瓘 jade cup.”

shuowen:84.text: Jade. Formed from 玉, with 敬 indicating the sound.

shuowen:85.text: Jade. Formed from 玉, with 典 indicating the sound.

shuowen:86.text: Jade. Formed from 玉, with 夒 indicating the sound. Read like 柔.

shuowen:87.text: Jade. Formed from 玉, with 毄 indicating the sound. Read like 鬲.

shuowen:88.text: 璵璠, the precious jade of Lu. Formed from 玉, with 番 indicating the sound. Confucius said: “Beautiful is 璵璠! Seen from afar, it is radiant; viewed closely, it is lustrous. In one respect its texture excels; in another its luster excels.”

shuowen:89.text: The jade called 璵璠. Formed from 玉, with 與 indicating the sound.

shuowen:90.text: 瑾瑜: beautiful jade. Formed from 玉, with 堇 indicating the sound.

shuowen:91.text: 瑾瑜: beautiful jade. Formed from 玉, with 俞 indicating the sound.

shuowen:92.text: Jade. Formed from 玉, with 工 indicating the sound.

shuowen:93.text: 𤦃瓄, a kind of jade. Formed from 玉, with 來 indicating the sound.

shuowen:94.text: Red jade. Formed from 玉, with 敻 indicating the sound.

shuowen:95.text: Jade. Formed from 玉, with 向 indicating the sound.

shuowen:96.text: Jade. Formed from 玉, with 剌 indicating the sound.

shuowen:97.text: The 珣玗琪 of Yiwulü, called “Yi jade” in the Book of Zhou. Formed from 玉, with 旬 indicating the sound. Another explanation says a vessel, pronounced like 宣.

shuowen:98.text: Jade. Formed from 玉, with 路 indicating the sound.

shuowen:99.text: Three parts jade and two parts stone. Formed from 玉, with 贊 indicating the sound. The Rites says: “The Son of Heaven uses 全, pure jade; high dukes use 駹, four parts jade and one stone; marquises use 瓚; earls use 埒, equal parts jade and stone.”

shuowen:100.text: The radiance of jade. Formed from 玉, with 英 indicating the sound.
